title: Two men, two worlds
hookLine: a Muslim mystic in love and a Roman emperor on duty: different aims, different gods, kept apart

cards: Put Marcus and Rumi in a room together and they'd barely understand each other. Still, after seventy-odd days, it's tempting to blend them. Both wise, both old, both on the inspiration shelf.

You could make a nice poster: Marcus says this, Rumi says that, same idea really. But they didn't share a language, a century, a god or a goal. They've been read side by side on purpose, and kept apart on purpose.
Before the camp closes, here's why. Two men, two worlds.

teach.h: AN EMPEROR, A MYSTIC, A THOUSAND YEARS.
teach.b: Start with the facts. Marcus Aurelius was a Roman emperor of the second century who wrote his notebook in Greek. Rumi was a Muslim scholar and mystic of the thirteenth century who wrote in Persian.
More than a thousand years stand between them.

teach.h: RUMI: FROM RUM, ONCE ROMAN LAND.
teach.b: There's even a small irony in the name: Rumi means of Rum, the name Muslims gave to Anatolia, because it had once been Roman land. That's the closest the two men come to touching. Marcus's world is Stoic.
The universe is ordered by reason, which he calls nature, or the gods, or Zeus.

teach.h: REASON AND DUTY; GOD AND LOVE.
teach.b: The good life is living in line with that reason: doing your duty, being just and kind, accepting what comes. He's honestly unsure what happens after death. Rumi's world is Islamic and Sufi.

There is one God, Allah, known through the Quran and the Prophet. The good life is love: the reed longing for the reedbed, the lover burning to meet the beloved. His whole poetry leans toward union with God.
So one man steadies himself; the other longs to be undone. One reaches for duty; the other for love.
When they seem to say the same thing, like accepting what comes, they mean it for different reasons and aim it at different ends.
Blending them would quietly erase both, the way many popular versions have stripped out Rumi's Islam.
Keeping them apart lets each be himself. You can learn from both without making them agree.

how: Careful readers of old texts keep each author in his own setting, reading Marcus as a Roman Stoic and Rumi as a Muslim Sufi, rather than blending them into one teaching.

o: an emperor and a mystic, read together, kept apart
a Roman and a Persian who once met in Konya
two wise teachers who taught the very same truth

s: Rumi and Marcus lived around the same time
more than a thousand years apart: a second-century emperor and a thirteenth-century mystic.
the name Rumi points back to Rome
Rum was the Muslim name for Anatolia, once Roman land.
when they both accept what comes, they mean the same thing
they mean it for different reasons: nature's reason for Marcus, love of God for Rumi.

games.q: someone makes a poster: "Marcus and Rumi taught the same truth." what do you say?
o: they lived different lives for different ends; learn from both, blend neither.
games.why: Marcus steadied himself by reason and duty; Rumi longed for union with God. keeping them apart lets each be himself, with no ranking.

practice: Bring back your Marcus line and let it stand on your left, in its tent by the Danube; bring back your Rumi story and let it stand on your right, in Konya, with the reed flute. Don't make them talk to each other.
Just let both be there, each whole.

wordCard.voice: Two men. A Roman emperor on duty and a Muslim mystic in love, a thousand years apart, read side by side and never merged. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: they don't merge. Each one gets to stay whole, and stay himself. See you tomorrow.
